source.quote:
The Greek infinitive is a verbal noun. It is not declined.
All infinitive morphemes, except for the present active and second aorist active, end in αι.
The infinitive has no time significance, only aspect: continuous; undefined; perfected.
The infinitive does not have a subject, but there will often be a word in the accusative functioning as if it were the subject.
An infinitive is most easily recognized as a verb preceded by the word "to."
It is always indeclinable (which means it has no case), but is viewed as singular neuter.
When it is preceded by a definite article, the article is always neuter singular and its case is determined by the function of the infinitive.
The infinitive has no person and no number!
Infinitives can occur in three tenses: present, aorist, perfect.
The present active infinitive ending is ειν. The present active infinitive of λύω is λύειν.
The present ("continuous") infinitive is built on the present tense stem.
The infinitive built on the present stem indicates a continuous action.
You may at first want to use "continue" in your translation of the present infinitive. βλέπειν means "to continue to see."
This is because ειν is actually a contraction of εεν.
